analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans buy cheaper insulin from licensed Canadian pharmacies and wholesalers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee after being referred there in February 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Food and Drug Administration to write rules, within 180 days, letting wholesalers, pharmacies, and individual patients import insulin from Canada. It set up a certification system for foreign pharmacies and wholesalers, required valid US prescriptions, allowed safety testing of imported insulin, and barred drug makers from raising prices or cutting supplies to block importation. After two years of demonstrated cost savings and safe access, the Health and Human Services Secretary could expand the program to other countries with comparable drug-approval standards.
analysis.who_benefits: People with diabetes who pay out of pocket for insulin, including the uninsured and those with high deductibles, who could buy the same or biosimilar insulin from certified Canadian sellers at Canadian prices. Wholesalers, pharmacies, and certified Canadian sellers would gain a new legal channel for cross-border sales.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to issue regulations within 180 days permitting wholesalers, pharmacies, and individuals to import qualifying insulin from Canada [S2] [S3].

Insulin must have the same active ingredient, strength, and route of administration as a US-approved product, come from FDA-registered facilities meeting good manufacturing practices, and carry English labeling [S3].
Individuals may import only for personal use and only with a valid US prescription from a licensed practitioner, dispensed by a certified foreign pharmacy [S3].

It is unlawful for manufacturers to charge certified foreign sellers higher prices, restrict or delay their insulin supplies, or alter the product for Canada in ways designed to defeat importation [S3].

The Secretary may suspend importation by any seller or importer that shows a pattern of counterfeit, recalled, or noncompliant drugs, and may approve laboratories for random testing of imported insulin [S3].

analysis.who_pays: US insulin manufacturers, which currently charge far higher prices in the United States than in Canada, would lose revenue as patients and buyers imported the same products at lower prices. The FDA and HHS bear the cost of running and enforcing the certification program, funded by fees on foreign sellers.

drawbacks.text: FDA and industry critics have long argued that personal drug importation is hard to police and can expose patients to counterfeit or substandard products; this bill responds with seller certification, prescription requirements, testing, and suspension authority, but a large cross-border channel would still be harder to oversee than the domestic supply chain [S3].

Importation attacks prices at the pharmacy counter but does nothing about the underlying list prices of insulin in the United States, so patients who rely on insurance formularies or who cannot navigate foreign pharmacies would see no benefit [S3].

The program depends on cooperation from Canadian authorities and sellers, and Canada's supply is limited; the bill only allows expansion to other countries after two years of evidence that Canadian importation produced savings and safe access [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients rationing insulin because of US prices, the upside is direct and large: the same or equivalent products at Canadian prices. The design is more careful than many importation bills, with prescription requirements, certification, testing, and recall rules. The main risks are enforcement burden at the FDA and the possibility that manufacturers use differential pricing or product changes to blunt the program, which the bill tries but may not fully prevent. The bigger limitation is scope: it addresses one drug class, not US drug prices generally.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee in early 2019 and never moved again; no committee vote, no floor vote, and the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch (D-VT) introduced the bill on February 28, 2019, joined by Rep. Francis Rooney (R-FL) as its sole cosponsor [S1] [S3] [S4].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction, and on March 1, 2019 it went to that committee's Health Subcommittee [S5].
No further action was taken for the rest of the 116th Congress: no hearings, markup, committee vote, or floor vote appear in the action history, and the Congress ended January 3, 2021 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US insulin manufacturers, which keep the price gap between the US and Canadian markets intact. Patients paying high insulin prices gained nothing from the bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insulin makers keeping US prices high

against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action; no markup or committee vote was ever held

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, so it was nominally bipartisan, but it died in committee without any recorded vote, leaving no party-line record to measure.

industries.industry: US insulin and brand-name drug manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would open a legal channel for the same or biosimilar insulin to be imported at Canadian prices, eroding the manufacturers' ability to charge much higher US prices. Its anti-discrimination and anti-circumvention provisions directly target manufacturer pricing and supply practices. Its failure leaves their US pricing intact.

The bill would create a certified-seller program letting licensed Canadian pharmacies and wholesalers legally sell insulin to Americans, with certification fees and FDA compliance duties. Their gain runs alongside patients' savings.

Registered US dispensers and wholesalers could import qualifying insulin, potentially lowering their acquisition costs; some would gain a competitive channel while others would face price competition on insulin they currently sell at US prices.
